utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I apologise for the late start today. At airports you always hear that is due to the late arrival of the plane while similar situations exist today. Mr. Margetts, are you ready to continue the examination of Mr. Lyntton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lyntton, I would like to remind that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lyntton.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As you are aware, your statement has now been admitted into evidence, and there is just a few matters that I'd like to go through with you in relation to the issues that you've already addressed in your statement. The first matter I'd like you to turn your mind to is the interview that you conducted with the elderly couple on the morning of the 25th of August, on your way to what you anticipated would be a meeting in the region of the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have the English transcript of Exhibit P871, that's 65 ter 5463, displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I don't have much to ask you about this particular interview, other than for you to look down this first page of this transcript here. And if you could identify for the Court whether or not this is the transcript of the interview that you conducted with that elderly couple.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, the reference to this interview and Mr. Lyntton's statement is in paragraph 9 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lyntton, is that a transcript of the interview you conducted with the elderly couple?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. If we could move on to the next issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Following that interview of the elder couple, you proceeded to the village where you anticipated there would be a meeting. In fact, the chief of police didn't arrive and you proceeded to interview one of the local villagers. Now, at some stage, you were informed that there was smoke in the valley, and the camera was turned towards those plumes of smoke. I'd just like to display for you on the screen some footage that was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if -- what we will, in fact, play now is a segment of P872, starting from counter reference 21 minutes, 54 seconds. And, Your Honours, for your reference, the reference to the plumes of smoke is in paragraph 13 of Mr. Lyntton's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Lyntton, is this footage of the plumes of smoke from the vantage point of the village where you met with the villagers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one there from the higher plain was from the village. This one to me seems as if we were on the way to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So where were you situated when this frame that's now displayed, which is at counter reference for the record 22 minutes, 22.5 seconds, where were you in the valley at that stage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, I would say, about halfway between the original starting point and our destination, which was the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, you referred to travelling from the initial village toward these plumes of smoke and you crossed a main road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was that main road in the valley?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And would it have been in the vicinity of this vantage point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you also referred in your statement to seeing some police vehicles located near that main road. Would have those police vehicles been in the vicinity of the vantage point that we see here, looking back to the plumes of smoke?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This angle, I would say, we may either have just passed those police vehicles or we may just be getting to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to now turn to footage you have as you proceeded toward -- footage that was shot as you proceeded towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if I could ask the case manager, please, to play -- to move forward on that video to the counter reference 23 minutes and 10.23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' reference, at paragraph 15 of Mr. Lyntton's statement, he refers to driving up a little stream to get to Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This footage that you've just seen, Mr. Lyntton, is that a depiction of the part of the drive you are referring to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to leave that topic and move to the interview that you conducted the next day with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have displayed on the screen Exhibit P504, and, in fact, the English transcript of that video interview, and if we could display page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lyntton, in your statement, you describe that -- the interview that you conducted with General Ivan Cermak, and here we have the transcript of that interview. First part of that interview I'd like to refer you to, you'll see in the middle of the page displayed on the left there in English. It's the bottom of the second answer that General Cermak provides; and he says, in reference to the village of Grubori, that one or two houses were burnt in the operation. Is that consistent with your observations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And your observations were that more or less houses were burnt?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: More.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Secondly, following on the next sentence, he says that one Serbian terrorist was arrested and one body was found, and he believes that body was the body of a Croatian army soldier because he had his hands tied with a wire behind his back? Now, just for clarification, you had been in the village that morning prior to interviewing General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Had you observed anything of the nature of what General Cermak describes there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could then move to the third answer that you see on that page, and it's down toward the bottom there. And he refers to the operation being conducted by special police, and he says: "And at that moment when they were fired at, our special forces returned the fire and, well, that returning of fire resulted in, well, wounding and it resulted in setting houses on fire." Now, whilst you were in Plavno valley, did you hear any gunshots?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We heard one gunshot the morning of, and during the first interview that we talked about just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that's audible on the videotape of that interview --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And apart from that, you didn't hear any exchange of fire in the valley?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And when you were observing the houses in the village of Grubori, was there anything you observed that suggested that the houses had been set on fire in the manner that General Cermak describes; that is, that the returning of fire resulted in the houses being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, the villages looked as though -- it wasn't like there was military fighting. It just looked as if someone had gone around, setting all the houses on fire. So, can you just rephrase the question? I'm not sure I totally understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, when you were there observing the houses, did you see any damage to the exterior of the houses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You mean like bullets, you know, gun-fire, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yeah. Anything consistent with a war operation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was just basically just burning houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the burning houses, was there anything that you observed that would suggest to you how they could have been ignited? I'm not suggesting that you're an expert in field; and, obviously, there's no need for you to venture into any opinions on this. It's just as a person being present in the village, you may be able to assist the Trial Chamber by what you observed about the nature of the fire inside the houses, and whether you made any observations about or -- about how the fires that you saw could have been ignited?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it looked to me every house almost or I think about half the houses had the window-frames were all burned or the roofs were either burning or had been burned. And to me, just in the back of my mind, it looked like someone had gone around with a flaming torch and just kind of chucked a torch inside every house that they fancied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could move now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might add, the doors, for example, none of the doors were off, everything was normal, except for the fact that the houses were burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 of the interview, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, if you see in the first answer provided by General Cermak on that page, he says that the Croatian civilian authorities got to this village - referring to Grubori - looked after the people, organised humanitarian assistance for them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's at the second paragraph that appears on the page on the left.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it's the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And he says that the authorities got to the village, they looked after the people, organised humanitarian assistance for them, and other assistance they need, and people stayed in their houses. Now, did you observe, either when you were there around about the middle of the day on the 25th of August or alternatively on the 26th August, did you observe any representatives of the Croatian authorities in the village?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in your discussion with villagers, did they make any reference to any humanitarian assistance they had been provided?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please scroll down on page 2 to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, just a note here, in your question at the bottom here, you're still referring to this topic of assistance provided, and you say: "Just one kilometre away ..." This is it the last question you ask on this page: "Just one kilometre away from the burning village, there were ten --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I haven't got this on my page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry. On the left, on the screen --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- you'll see the last -- the last full question. The reference is to Grubori at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And then there's your question that proceeds Cermak -- General Cermak's previous answer, and it commences: "Can you tell him --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What I'm do is I'm referring down to part way through the second sentence. So starting at the end of the second line, there's a reference that says: "Just one kilometre away from the burning village, there were ten Croatian police vehicles," and you say -- you ask a question as to why they could not help the people who were remaining there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Registrar, if I could please refer over to page 3, and to the top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, once again, this is your second question here. You say: "We're talking about six hours after the burning started. There were ten empty Croatian police vehicles," and you ask General Cermak how they could ignore the burning of the village. Now, then General Cermak answers you, and he says: "Look, I don't know. He asked me today. The gentleman put the question to me today. He said , 'Today I saw six police cars ... of this village. I wasn't there. I couldn't see that. I can only tell the gentleman one thing. Had we wanted to cover up anything,'" and then the answer continues. Now, at any time during your meeting with General Cermak, did you refer to the presence of six police vehicles or are the references that are recorded on this transcript to ten police vehicles the only references you made to General Cermak about the number of police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This was the first time I had mentioned the number of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, did anyone else in your team, your production crew or to your knowledge anyone else that met with General Cermak during the preparation for the interview or the conduct of the interview, mention the number of six police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The -- I don't have any further questions about the interview with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In your statement, you refer to the fact that following the interview of General Cermak, you packaged up all of the footage that you had taken, the footage in the valley and also the footage of the interview; and you arranged for that to be transported to Zagreb by helicopter, and you then proceeded by road back to Zagreb. Why did you arrange for the footage to be transported separately by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were scared. The whole assignment -- I had in the back of my mind that a BBC cameraman, maybe six months or maybe a year before, had been shot for taking pictures of pillaging in the north of Croatia. And to my mind, what we had shot that day was ten times more, maybe a 100 times more potent than just some pillaging. Plus, we had an interview with General Cermak, and we were going to be on our own leaving the area. So it made sense that we handed the goods, as it were, over to the UN, the military and they could get it out, because the helicopters landed in Knin. There was regular flights to Knin. So we knew that, and I knew that one would be leaving that day, probably. So that's why we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You referred to the -- you said what you had was 100 times more potent, and you said, than just some pillaging. Then you continue on: "Plus, we had an interview with General Cermak ..." Can you just explain a bit further, what was the nature of the footage that you had and the nature of the interview that you had conducted that in your mind made this footage potent, sufficient for it to be transported separate to yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, ethnic cleansing had been in the lexicon for some time now, and I had never seen anything like that and this was pretty much the first time I had seen something like that. So not only did we have -- I mean, we were there it must have been just maybe a couple of hours after the assault or whatever, you know, whatever it was took place in the village; then we had pictures of -- of dead bodies; and then we had an interview with what I presumed was the local commander, General Cermak, categorically denying any such activity. And I just -- you know, I had been there, I had seen it two hours before I spoke to him. So to me, as a journalist, as a story, you know, it was like a perfect story. I had the evidence and then I had the denial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: A little further on in your statement, you also referred to the fact that after you had driven out of Knin, some vehicles approached you from behind. Can you just explain to the Court what happened there, what the nature of the vehicles was, and what you did when -- when those vehicles approached from behind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we decided that we wanted to get out of there as soon as possible. It was probably a three-hour drive maybe to -- I mean two-hours to Split, to the coast, to the sort of normalization of Croatia, you know, the seaside bit. And as we drove out of that area, we saw two or three more little hamlets alight, and this was dusk. So you got to imagine you're driving down a desolate road and there are still burning villages. So it's not like the fact that we shot some footage and had an interview with a military commander had changed anything. It seemed to still be going on. But, then, in my -- in my mirror, I saw literally between ten and 15 white, again white, sort of mini-van type vehicles approaching behind us. And I didn't know who they were, where they were going, if they were trying to find us because we shot this footage. You know, you just don't know in that situation. So, at first, we sped up a bit. We thought maybe we can, you know, outrun these guys just in case it's us they're looking for, which may seem a little overdramatic but, you know, we just didn't know. We just wanted to get out of there. Then we thought, no, probably they -- you know, they don't want us. We'll just pull over. So we pulled over to the side of the road, and they just went past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And just my last question is just after you returned to Zagreb, was any of the footage that you had shot shown on any commercial television networks; and, if so, what parts of the footage were shown?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My managing editor of UN TV, Roy Head, he -- he basically sent the package or some of the package, some raw footage, to the networks. I mean BBC, CNN, Sky News UK. And probably two or three days later, I actually was at home in Zagreb in my apartment, and I saw a sort of 20-, 30-second report that, in fact, there was some claims of ethnic cleansing on the Croatian side. I don't remember exactly, but they used the burning house, they used the old lady in my piece, and they used I think just a brief shot of General Cermak denying that -- that there were old people in villages in their pyjamas being taken out and shot. The sort of denial bit of the interview that he knew anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lyntton. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Who will be the first? It will be you Ms. Higgins? Mr. Lyntton, you will be cross-examined by Ms. Higgins, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lyntton, by October 1994, it's correct, isn't it, that you had left the military after five years of service and you joined the UN TV?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And by August 1995, your job was as a producer for UN TV?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, we've seen from the films that you have provided to the Prosecution that perhaps, as well as being the producer, you were always -- you were rather also involved in the direction of those films, very hands on. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And sometimes in the role that you performed for UN TV, you would be involved, presumably, in researching your stories and the people that were going to be taking part in your features. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes -- there was the case sometimes I was simply given an assignment and other people at UN TV would have picked out interviews for me to go and cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'll going to leave a slight pause because we have to take account of the translation, interpretation issues. You would be assigned specific stories by the head of operations in Zagreb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The managing editor, I mean head of operations, to me, suggests military or UN; but this was the UN TV managing editor, and, obviously, he had some contact with the press and information, chief of press and information of UNPROFOR. But my stories or my assignments came from the UN TV managing editor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry if I misspoke. That was my intention to reflect that it was coming from within the UN TV itself.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And the average length of your assignments could vary from days to weeks or --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, one day to maybe a week in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, I want to deal firstly with your arrival in Knin, and it's right that in these proceedings the only statement you have given is dated back in October 2001; I think you'll recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, obviously, that was more than six years after the events that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I would be very interested to know if you have any notes from the time particularly of the 25th and the 26th of August that you could help us with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Any diary that you kept for that period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I know you've had the opportunity to look at detail in your -- about your statement and what you wrote. Can you help us with the date, perhaps, on which you travelled down with your team to Knin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived on the Thursday -- the Thursday or the Friday morning. So it was the 20 -- it was either the evening of the 24th or the morning of the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, in fact, in your statement, you refer to the following morning, "my team accompanied Edward Flynn," so that would suggest then perhaps the day before, then, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Was it your first trip to Knin --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- as an UN producer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: After you left on the 26th, when you travelled back up to Zagreb, did you subsequently visit Knin or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. Within the institution of UN TV, can you help me with this, as to whether or not you ever received any sort of briefing about the situation in Knin post-Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, UN TV is -- was situated in headquarters UNPROFOR Zagreb, so we had access to a lot of information, press briefings, and our own contacts on the ground. So there was no formal briefing; but, obviously, I had been keeping abreast of what was going on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So no formal briefing but UN TV?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just -- we think that some Serbs have tried to stay behind, please go and see if can you get a nice positive story about, you know, the fact that the Croatians are -- have invited and have welcomed the Serbs as staying behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, one of your main contacts in Knin was also UN press officer, is that right, Mr. Roberts? Do you know him, Mr. Alun Roberts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall contact with him. We would have gone through his office to get down there and arrange permissions, but I can't recall any contact. I think he may have even been not around at that stage because I know the name very well. But one of the issues we had down there was that there was no press and info people to really happy us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah. It's just that you say in your statement that your main contact was the UN press and information office, and the officer there was Mr. Roberts. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall whether what I meant by that was simply that we arranged to go through his office, but the only people I remember dealing with down there when we got there were the -- the humanitarian officer, Flynn, and a sort of battalion commander-type rank of major or colonel, who, again, was helping. He was the one that was helping us get the interview with General Cermak's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a few questions about Mr. Cermak because, obviously, you have written about him in your statement. Before you arrived in Knin on the 24th of August, is it right that you had never met Mr. Cermak before? That's right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Before you arrived in Knin, did you know who Mr. Cermak was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I knew in Zagreb that the military governor was General Cermak; but definitely when we got there, the name kept coming up: "You got to see Cermak. You got to see Cermak. Go and get an interview with him."

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: When was the first -- was the first time that you met Mr. Flynn when you were done in Knin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, we know that you knew about Mr. Cermak being, as you call, the military governor from him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You said that yourself in your supplementary statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. But if -- you know, I can't remember whether that -- you know, you asked did I know who he was. You know, maybe someone in Zagreb, maybe my boss, had said the new -- the new guy down there to talk to is General Cermak. He may have said that to me because you got to remember this was such a swift regime change, as it were. We had been used to dealing with Serbs in Knin, UN TV. So we knew all the personalities of the Croatian Serbs down there, but we didn't know any of the new Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand. I'm just trying to establish from your supplemental statement that you gave to the Prosecution on Sunday --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- we know that it was Mr. Flynn who told you that Mr. Cermak was the military governor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I see my learned friend on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. It's just that my learned friend is referring to a supplemental information sheet that we prepared following the proofing. I just refer to paragraph 4 of that, and maybe my learned friend could refer to the precise reference that is made to the persons that informed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, I'm coming on that to that, Your Honour. If I can deal with it in my way, I'll address the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to a supplemental statement the Chamber is not aware of; so, therefore, one way or the other, either you read it or -- but we are not able to follow what the testimony is about if you refer to an unknown document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the assistance of the Bench, I'm going to read the line and give the witness the opportunity to listen to that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The line is as follows, Mr. Lyntton: Edward Flynn and the UN representative informed the witness that General Cermak was the military governor in charge of the area." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you give me the name of the UN representative while we're on the subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember who that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right. Can you let me know why it is that you hadn't explained where you got the information from about Mr. Cermak being, as you say, a military governor, why that wasn't put in your 2001 statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that -- that original statement was what I could remember at the time. I don't think anyone specifically asked me that question you just asked me. So the -- what I was trying to do during the statement was just remember who I had come into contact with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to look in a little bit more detail in a moment about your statement, but if we could just stay with the issue of military governor for the moment. In your role as a TV producer, director for UN TV --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- did you ever yourself conduct research into Mr. Cermak's position, function, responsibilities; or was there simply not an occasion to do so --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- within the limitation of your time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever question or have the opportunity to question, again, given the limited time you were there, the information that you had been given by Mr. Flynn and the UN representative that Mr. Cermak was the so-called military governor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, it is not intended as any criticism because, again, I understand how long you were in Knin, would it be fair to say that you didn't have any particular detailed knowledge of the working of the Croatian military structure down in that particular area at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be fair, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And we know from what you have told us that it would be accurate to say you only met Mr. Cermak once during the interview you had with him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Correct. And, again, just for the record, duration of approximately 30 minutes, something like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's also correct, isn't it - and we've got the transcript that you have had a chance to look through; I'm trying to be fair to you, Mr. Lyntton -- that he, in fact, himself never described himself as the military governor to you during the time you met him? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that may not be correct in the sense that there was some chitchat beforehand, and he may have said, you know, "My name is General Cermak and I'm the commander here." Like one word, if you were introducing yourself in that kind of position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We're in a court of law here, and I think you would agree with me that you are not able to confirm that he did, in fact, say he was military governor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You can't tell me that he said that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- can you? Okay. Now, again, prefacing this with the limited knowledge that I know you had, no criticism intended, did you ever come to know, either at the time or subsequently through your contacts with the Prosecution, that there was, in fact, no such position as military governor in the Croatian army? Did you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the structure or the functioning of the Ministry of Interior in Croatia in that region at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just testing again the remit of what you can speak about, Mr. Lyntton.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know, for example, the name of the local police commander in Knin at the police station?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware there was even a police commander. I mean, this was again -- this was two or three days after. It seemed to me that, you know, personalities were -- you know, they weren't even -- the buildings, you know, we didn't even know which buildings people were in, let alone that, "Oh, yes, there's a new police commander." So, no, I didn't know that there would have been one there on those dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you were there for only two days?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to complete the circle, I presume it is also correct that you are not able to tell me in any detail about the hierarchy or workings of the military police in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So just to recap, the sole source, having considered where we've got to at this point, for your assertion or conclusion that Mr. Cermak was the military governor was Mr. Flynn, in fact, and the unnamed UN representative. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. Because if I write someone's name on the screen, I need to get their title as well. So, although I cannot remember if I specifically asked this, when we arrived at the building where Cermak was in the centre of Knin, and when we took his details as one would, I am almost certain I would have said, "Well, what shall we call you?" So someone, I'm not suggesting it was General Cermak himself, but somehow I must have got a title because I knew I would need that for my piece.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, to be fair to you, Mr. Lyntton, you've told us how you got that title and we know you were in contact with Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That's fair isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The first time that title was mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And for your purposes, that would be a title that you would presumably write down and use.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I also think I would have checked during the interview what the gentleman -- what the General wants to be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, you say you would have, but let's get this straight. You're not telling me, are you, that Mr. Cermak said to you, "Hello, I'm the military governor." You can't say that in this court, can you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but it may have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to that you it wasn't possible, Mr. Lyntton, but let's move on. I don't think you can really contradict me, can you? The most you can say is "may"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: May, absolutely, but not definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, don't you think that if Mr. Cermak had have said that, that might have been something important that you would have, A, brought to the attention of the Prosecution in your Sunday or weekend briefing; or, B, put into some sort of statement format back in 2001?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because until you brought it up, the fact that we -- and, again, this is sometimes a linguistic issue, the fact that we brought up today "military governor." I mean, for me, you know, commander, head of -- you know, it could have been anything. But that was simply a term that would have been -- that I used; and as I say, I'm sure that I would have checked what General Cermak wanted to be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You didn't make any notes, did you, at the time you gave -- you made the interview with Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have made some notes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Where are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got them now. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you can't help me with what was actually said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you ever come to know in your research, again as a producer, either at the time or subsequently, that Mr. Cermak was, in fact, a civilian businessman who was appointed, not as a military governor, but as a garrison commander of Knin appointed by President Tudjman on the 5th? Did you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I came to know was that an independent newspaper journalist had told me that -- that he had a string of brothels in Zagreb, and I did not know that he was a businessman.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right. Let take this back a little, shall we? Now, you mentioned brothels for the first time in your statement that you made in 2001. And in that statement - I'm sure you have it before you - paragraph 27 on page 5, at the bottom, you say that you recognised Cermak's main body-guard who was the owner of a brothel in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I don't believe that the witness does have the statement before him. It is P870.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps my learned friend can provide him with a copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I don't have an unmarked copy in my possession. I'll just check whether my learned friend does. Yes, if I could provide it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If could you have a look in the statement at paragraph 27, please, you see there the reference to: "I recognised Cermak's main body-guard who was the owner of a brothel in Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, this brothel in Zagreb, was that near the UN base in Vela Kugarica [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, this brothel, was --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time I went there was with the independent newspaper journalist as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: She asked me -- she went to UN TV and said, "Is there anyone who would come with me? I'm doing a story on brothels in Zagreb. Could I borrow somebody who is an interpreter?" And my boss asked me if I could go with her because I was -- you know, we were both from London and could I help her out. So I just want to it make I want clear, I wasn't going there to use the ladies there. I was just going to help because she was female, the journalist. I was just going as a bit of, you know, sort of moral support and to be her interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That is very gallant of you, Mr. Lyntton, if I may say.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would it be, perhaps, preferable to suggest that this brothel was more of a disco bar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if you looked at it, that's what you would say, but I knew from other people that that's what it was used for.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You're not honestly coming to this courtroom and suggesting for the first time that you know that Mr. Cermak had a string of brothels in Zagreb. Is that what you're honestly coming here to say, Mr. Lyntton, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You asked me did I subsequently find out, so all I said was that the journalist told me that that's what he had. So I don't know that, but that's what I was -- that's what someone told me, because you said did you find out subsequently and that's why I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Name of the journalist, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You, as a professional producer and director, your sources are important, Mr. Lyntton, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You're willing to come here and report rumour and gossip about somebody's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, you asked what Mr. Lyntton found out later. There was no limitation to his journalistic work, where, of course, would you require from someone to check all his sources. You came with a very general question, the witness answered that, and then to treat him in this way is not what I expect to you do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was whether he was, in fact, a civilian businessman, and I appreciate Your Honours' observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What he found out about that. I'm not saying what did you observe the yourself, what he found out, in a very general way; then he answered that question; and if you say, "Have you further investigated that," fine, put all questions. But the tone you used in relation to this was unfair, taking into account how the issue came up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will amend my tone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Lyntton, have you ever been shown the document appointing Mr. Cermak to the position of garrison commander by the Prosecution during your time here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can you assist us with how many staff the garrison had or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few. I remember walking into the building, and I just remember thinking, "Where is everybody?"

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know that the position of garrison commander was a non-operational position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: From your contact with Mr. Edward Flynn, did you know the role that Mr. Cermak had been assigned concerning the normalization of life in the area, assisting the UN, and assisting in relation to the displaced persons? Did you come to know about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, just while we're dealing with descriptions of Mr. Cermak, another description that you used was the following: In your statement, and you can take it from me or check as you need to, you say: "I think Cermak was a policeman who had been bumped up into the army." Can you help with who told that you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know that that information was, in fact, as inaccurate as the information you had about him being a military governor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right to say that in your capacity, and given again the limited contact you had with people down there and the two days you spent, that you never, in fact, came to know what he was in charge of or what his real title was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm trying to be a little bit fairer and nicer. Now, let's move on, if I can, to the 25th, please, of August. You have already told me that you don't have any notes from that time, but I know you have a recollection and we've got your 2001 statement. On the 25th, your UN TV team, which I think consisted of three people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You accompanied Mr. Flynn and his interpreter to a meeting in Plavno valley. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you may not remember all the names, but I think you might remember that there were other people present as well. You might -- do you remember a Mr. Roberts? I have asked you about him already.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And an UN CIVPOL member, a man called Mr. Romasev?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember a UN CIVPOL guy being there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And a lady, Maria Teresa Mauro, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But we have seen from your footage that there were, in fact, a convoy of you who went up to the village in Grubori. We have seen the three cars. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were just two cars. It was us and the UN humanitarian officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That can be checked --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been someone else with us, behind coming up, because we were all heading that way, but I don't remember. All I remember is it being us and the UN humanitarian officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, as we have heard, during that meeting at some point, smoke is brought to your attention and you move up in convoy to Grubori village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What I'd like to just ask you briefly is if you can assist me with the timing of your arrival in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: To remind you, you said in your 2001 statement that it was about 11.00, 11.30?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the Court here has received evidence of different timings between 1330 and 1430?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And I wonder if could you assist us at all with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, what happened that morning, we would have left at about 8.00. We got the first interview with the couple on the road. Then we got to the -- the first village where the meeting was supposed to take place, and it was supposed to take place at about 10.00. So, by the time we waited around, no appearance of the Croatian chief of police, by the time we then saw the smoke -- did you ask when we first saw the smoke or when we got to Grubori village?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No. When you got to Grubori village, where it could have been later than 11.30 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been. It could have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, after your visit to Grubori village, you returned to Knin without Flynn sometime in the afternoon. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That's what you said in your statement, that you returned without him and he was still up in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In fact, when I looked at the -- over there last weekend, I realized that we had, in fact, gone back to the village the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come on to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'll come on that. You are absolutely right from your correction. What I'm asking you about is on the 25th, when you go up there --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- in your 2001 statement --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- you refer to you leaving to go back to Knin --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- and Flynn remaining?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: He then comes back later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we didn't go up a second time that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No. Exactly. I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you come to know that Mr. Flynn with others went to report to the office of Mr. Cermak, to a man called Dondo, once he had returned back in the afternoon of the 25th? Did you come to know that at some point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. But by the time you left Grubori on the 25th --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- you had not seen the two bodies at that point, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We also know, and you may correct me if I'm wrong, or had come to know that Mr. Flynn returned to Grubori a second time that day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: He then returned to Knin later that evening?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And is it right that he then told you later that evening about the two bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you can't help me, can you, with what Mr. Flynn reported to a man called Mr. Dondo at the office of Mr. Cermak, that afternoon after his first visit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I assume you cannot help me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you weren't present when that report was made to Mr. Cermak's office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time, and I don't know Your Honours's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we had a late start, perhaps I first inquire with you, how much time do you still need approximately so that I can make better planning for the morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I estimate 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another 30 minutes, yes. And other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have 30 to 45 minutes myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Then I suggest, Ms. Higgins, that you finish in the next 30 minutes, and that after the break, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that you will cross-examine the witness, so that we might not need a second break, because I understand, Mr. Margetts, that your next witness is not available today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, most likely, we will then finish in the second part of the hearing this morning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to deal with the interview that you had with Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just a few preliminary questions I want to deal with first with you. You have provided a proofing -- what we call a proofing note. It's a note that contains additional information and corrections that you made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And that's pursuant to your meetings just the previous weekend with the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, we also heard during your examination-in-chief that you made some corrections concerning the interview. The main corrections, just want to see if you'll agree with me, was firstly the date of the interview. You corrected it from being on the 25th, which is what you had originally said, to the 26th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Correct. You corrected the time of the UN interview, which you had said was at 4.00 on the 25th, and you now put at 11.30ish on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you also corrected the language used during the interview. You now accept that there was a Croatian interpreter present to interpret for the purposes of Mr. Cermak understanding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I don't have any dispute with your corrections as they stand at all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But what I don't understand and what I'd like you to try and help me with is how you came to make such effectively quite fundamental mistakes about this aspect of your testimony, back in 2001. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- it was a long time after, I was in the middle of my life after Bosnia, and I gave the statement I did on 2001. And when I looked at the footage again and the interview, I remember asking -- I saw that I had asked a specific question to General Cermak, and I said something like, "Do you recall or do you know anything about old men or old people being taken out in their pyjamas and being shot?" And once I had seen that again, I realized that I must have gone for the interview after we had been back that second time. So that's how I know that it was afterwards and not before. And as for why I didn't get that originally, it was just hard to remember the events exactly because there was so much going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: When was it that you came to review that footage and make that correction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you helped with the timing of the interview itself by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I mean, I worked it out if we went that morning to Grubori for the second time, the only thing we did -- you know, we sort of came straight back from Grubori to do the interview, which is why I said it was probably about is 11.30 because we were up there for an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of going to Mr. Cermak's office and having the interview with him, were you told by Mr. Flynn that as far as the UN were concerned, Mr. Cermak's door was always open to assist with anything that the UN needed assistance with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But I think it's right, and again you can review your 2001 statement, that during the interview, you concluded yourself that, to use your words, Mr. Cermak wanted to please and cooperate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And he engaged in what you refer to as small pleasantries before and after the interview with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, concerning your impression about that interview --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- in your 2001 statement, I'm going to read the passage to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You say the following: "Cermak presented himself as the commander of the area. It was clear from talking to him that I was talking to the man that was in charge of security for the area. He was wearing a green army shirt at the time of the interview."

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And that's at page 5, paragraph 3 of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's look a little more closely, if we may, at the conclusion that you drew?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be helpful, I think, if the witness read the full paragraph 28, because a portion of it, a small portion but a portion nonetheless, was omitted from the quotation. So I would be please if my learned friend could invite him to read paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually, the party questioning the witness chooses itself what portion to read, unless that gives a distorted picture of what was quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That would be our submission, Your Honour, to put it expressly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not my intention. I will read the whole piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Lyntton, just you can have a recap of what was said: "There were small pleasantries before and after the interview. Cermak presented himself as a the commander of the area, and that is why he would give us an interview. It was clear from talking to him that I was talking to the man that was in charge of security for the area. He was wearing a green army shirt at the time of the interview." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, your assessment, again, cold light of day now -- we know you were there for two days, we know what your specific and different function was as a producer. Cold light of day, your assessment of Mr. Cermak, as the commander of the area, was based on the following, I would suggest, and I would ask to you consider this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One, he had a rank; you called him General.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Two, he wore a military uniform. That had an impact, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Three, you had been told he was a military governor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right. Now, you also say that it was your impression, to use your words, that "this guy was in charge and clearly knew what was going on in his area." I'd like to us examine that a little more closely, and now turn to the actual interview itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If that could be pulled up on to the screen. Your Honour, I think that is P504.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the interview transcript yourself in front of you so that can you flick to it, Mr. Lyntton?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this it? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No. The witness has a copy of his statement. We'll attempt to furnish him with a hard copy of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, we have the first page, which will be sufficient for my purposes until you're provided with a copy. You can see there that the interview begins with two pieces or two tranches of information that Mr. Cermak gives to you before you launch into the substance of your interview. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: He just gave you, just to recap - we looked at the detail - he gave you some information about mopping-up operations towards the axes of villages of Plavno and Grubori and what had been found there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And he gave you information that one or two houses were burnt, Serb terrorists arrested, and a body found. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that interview, I think you would agree with me that he didn't tell you at any point where he got that information from. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you didn't know where that information came from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you couldn't know or didn't know at that time that he was passing on information to you that he had received himself. Fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to you telling him about Grubori itself. On that first page --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we can just scan down, please, to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You tell him about the 20 houses alight and the two dead old men. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I want to put this, Mr. Lyntton, into a context, and I'd ask you to try and look at this document with fresh eyes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I know it's difficult because it is your document, it's your interview. But just coming again to it in the cold light of day, if we can try?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It was said, just to put it in context for you, by Mr. Margetts, who summarized the evidence that you were to give to this Court, that Mr. Cermak denied old people were forced out of their homes and denied any one was shot at close quarters in Grubori during the course of this interview?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall that summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Going back to the interview, once you had told Mr. Cermak about the 20 houses and the two dead old men, let's just consider the two of us, if we may, the context of Mr. Cermak's responses to the information you kindly provide to him from what you saw, all right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: First page of this interview, five lines up, if you follow with me, at the end of that line, he says: "I don't know where he got this information from." He's referring to you there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page two of this interview, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, from the top, you provide him in paragraph 1 with more background, more information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: He says to you the words in paragraph 2: "I don't know where this gentleman had this information from about two civilians killed." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 2, fourth paragraph, if you can follow with me, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, you'll see the words there twice: "I don't know," in the first line, and in the third line: "I don't know." Do you see that, Mr. Lyntton?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, in paragraph 4: "I don't know if this morning there was anybody with the people up there." Do you see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 2, again, para 4: "I really don't have any information about these two bodies." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The bottom line of this page, he actually asks you for clarification: "What village? What police forces are you talking about?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you clarify again for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 3, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: "Look, I don't know." You see that reference there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like you to consider, looking at this interview in the round, and also looking at the fact of the placing of the information he gives you and once you tell him, what he says to you. All right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would it perhaps be more accuracy to say or fairer to say that rather than denying what had happened, when you told him the detail that you knew and you'd seen, didn't it become, in fact, clear, or perhaps it's now clear to you, that during the course of that interview and given his responses, he didn't actually know at that time the extent of what had happened up there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, at face value, you see, however, what he said to you about his lack of knowledge. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah. Another claim that you make, which I'd like to deal with briefly, is you say in your statement that you found it suspicious that he had appeared to be in command of the previous incidents and situation, but was equally willing suddenly to say that he was prepared to investigate a rumour brought to him by an UN TV producer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just say that again?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yeah, of course. He appeared to be in command of the previous incidents and situation, but was equally willing suddenly to say that he was prepared to investigate a rumour brought to him by an UN TV producer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: So did you ask if I was surprised about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No. Just coming on to deal with that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- so you understand where I'm moving to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, looking at this now, over 13 years later, given the context of who you were, what you were doing down there, and the limited duration of time you spent down there, is it, in fact, the case that you were never actually in the position to know the remit of his authority in that area? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That's not fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Why is that not fair?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just remember being in that room and getting -- you get a feeling when someone is not giving you the whole story, and the reason the interview lasted so long is because I just felt that I wasn't getting the true picture and I felt that there was something that he wasn't being open about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just a feel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That was just your feeling, nothing more?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Nothing to substantiate that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD LYNTTON [Resumed]
